screens.title: Polymorphism and Abstract Classes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two complementary ideas that make object-oriented Python code both flexible and reliable. First, polymorphism lets code operate on different kinds of objects through a shared behavior rather than a fixed type. Python’s dynamic duck typing is a practical example: if an object provides the methods your code needs, it will work regardless of the object's class. Second, Abstract Base Classes offer a stricter option when you need guarantees: they let you declare methods that every concrete subclass must implement, preventing accidental omissions. You will see simple, concrete examples: an animal speak demonstration that shows polymorphic calls in plain Python, operator behavior that adapts to operand types, and an ABC-based Shape example that demonstrates how the abc module and the @abstractmethod decorator protect your design. We will also practice by building a small payment processor that uses an abstract PaymentMethod interface. By the end of this chapter you’ll know when to rely on duck typing for fast, flexible code, and when to use ABCs to enforce contracts and catch errors early. Think about a plugin or payment system in your own projects and where each approach would fit.

Polymorphism and Abstract Classes
Understand duck typing, method overriding, and when to apply Abstract Base Classes.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

  • Walk through a Shape ABC and see how @abstractmethod enforces contracts.

Why it matters

Polymorphism keeps code generic and reusable. ABCs avoid runtime surprises by forcing implementations to provide required behavior. Together they help you design systems that are both flexible and robust.

screens.title: Polymorphism and Duck Typing
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism literally means many forms. In programming that translates to the ability of different objects to respond to the same operation in their own way. In Python this is most often expressed through duck typing. The essential claim of duck typing is that you do not need the object to be of a particular declared type; you only need it to provide the required behavior. A concise concrete example is animals with a speak method. A Dog, Cat, and Duck all implement speak in their own way. A generic function that calls speak on a passed object will produce different results depending on the object's implementation, and that is polymorphism in action. One common misconception is thinking polymorphism requires inheritance. It does not: two unrelated classes that both implement the same method are polymorphic for the purposes of code that calls that method. Another contrast is static typed languages where interfaces or base classes are often declared ahead of time; Python prefers behavior over formal type declarations but still allows structured enforcement when needed. A practical takeaway is to design small, well-documented method contracts so callers can rely on behavior. Question for reflection: when would you prefer the freedom of duck typing over the assurance of an enforced interface?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Polymorphism: objects provide the same method names and thus can be used interchangeably by calling code.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Polymorphism & Duck Typing
Core Concept
Polymorphism via behaviour
If an object provides the methods you need, your code will work with it.
# Example: three unrelated classes that all implement speak
class Dog:
  def speak(self):
    return "Woof!"

class Cat:
  def speak(self):
    return "Meow!"

class Duck:
  def speak(self):
    return "Quack!"

# A single function works with all of them
def make_animal_speak(animal):
  print(animal.speak())

make_animal_speak(Dog())
make_animal_speak(Cat())
make_animal_speak(Duck())
Explanation
  • Polymorphism relies on shared method names, not shared inheritance.
  • Duck typing means compatibility is checked by behavior, at runtime.
  • Design small, explicit method contracts to make duck-typed code reliable.
Example
The make_animal_speak function calls speak on any object that provides it; no base class is required.
Common misconception
Polymorphism does not always require inheritance. Two unrelated classes can be polymorphic as long as they provide the same methods.
Key Takeaway

Write interfaces by behavior. Use clear method names so polymorphic code remains readable and maintainable.

screens.title: make_animal_speak Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the make_animal_speak example line by line and see how Python resolves the call at runtime. The function takes a parameter called animal and calls the speak method. Python looks up the attribute speak on the passed object and then executes the bound method. The important observation is that lookup happens on the concrete object, not on the expected type. In practice this means the same function adapts to any object that exposes the method. A concrete scenario: you may have a list of different device objects that all implement a status method; a single monitoring loop can call status on each device without type checks. A common error is assuming that duck typing eliminates the need for documentation. In reality you should document the expected methods and their signatures so callers and implementers agree. Another pitfall is assuming a missing method will raise a friendly error; instead Python will raise an AttributeError at the point of use. A practical debugging approach is to rely on tests that instantiate representative concrete types and call the shared A P I. Takeaway: duck typing is powerful, but document and test the method contract to avoid runtime surprises.

keyIdea.title: Runtime dispatch
keyIdea.text: Method calls are resolved on the concrete object at runtime; the function only needs the expected behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › make_animal_speak Walkthrough
Code Walkthrough
def make_animal_speak(animal):
  # At runtime Python looks up 'speak' on the concrete object
  print(animal.speak())

# Usage with different objects
make_animal_speak(Dog())   # Woof!
make_animal_speak(Cat())   # Meow!
make_animal_speak(Duck())  # Quack!
When the function calls the method, Python performs attribute lookup on the concrete object. This is different from static binding in some other languages.
Example scenario
A monitoring loop calling status on heterogeneous device objects that all implement status.
Common mistake
Skipping documentation of the expected method signature and then encountering an AttributeError at runtime.
Tips
  • Document the expected method name and arguments for duck-typed APIs.
  • Use unit tests that exercise representative concrete implementations.
  • Use isinstance or hasattr sparingly — prefer a clear contract and tests.
Key Takeaway

Duck typing is simple and powerful — but it requires clear expectations and tests to avoid runtime errors.

screens.title: Operator Overloading and Special Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Python supports polymorphic operator behaviour through special methods. That means an operator such as plus or multiply delegates to a method like add or mul on the left operand. For built-in types this implements sensible behaviours: plus adds numbers and concatenates strings. You can also implement these special methods in your own classes to make operators behave meaningfully for custom types. A concrete example: implementing add for a Vector class so that the plus operator returns a new vector. A common misconception is that operator overloading magically makes code clearer. Overloading should be used to express natural arithmetic or combination semantics; otherwise it can confuse readers. When you design special methods, document their expected semantics and ensure they follow usual conventions like returning a new object for immutable types. In addition to add, methods like str and repr also shape how objects present themselves. The takeaway is to use operator overloading to make domain objects feel native to Python, but prefer explicit method names when behaviour could be surprising. Operator Overloading and Special Methods means operators call special methods on operands; classes can implement these to customize operator behaviour.. In practical terms, how operators adapt to operand types and how classes can customize behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Operator Overloading
Comparison: built-in vs custom
# Built-in polymorphism
1 + 2        # 3  (numeric addition)
'hello' + 'world'  # 'helloworld' (string concatenation)

# Customizing in a class
class Vector:
  def __init__(self, x, y):
    self.x = x
    self.y = y
  def __add__(self, other):
    return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)
When you implement __add__, the plus operator expresses vector addition in a natural way for that domain.
Guidelines
  • Overload operators only when the meaning is obvious and consistent.
  • Document semantics and expected operand types to prevent surprises.
  • Follow Python conventions: prefer returning new objects for immutable semantics.
Pro tip
Implement __repr__ or __str__ so debugging and interactive use are easier when you overload operators.
Key Takeaway

Operator overloading offers expressive domain modelling but must be used judiciously and documented clearly.

screens.title: Method Overriding
screens.narratorSegment: Method overriding is a focused form of polymorphism: a subclass provides its own implementation of a method that is defined in a superclass. This allows a generic base class to declare an operation and concrete subclasses to tailor the implementation. For example, a base Animal class might define a speak method that raises NotImplementedError or provides a generic behavior; Dog and Cat subclasses override speak with concrete sounds. Unlike duck typing, overriding typically involves an inheritance relationship, but the idea remains the same: different objects respond in different ways to the same method call. One misconception is to override methods without calling the superclass when the superclass contains important initialization or shared behavior; in such cases you should call super(). Another nuance is that overriding can be used to specialize validation or error checking while still reusing shared logic. The practical pattern is to design base classes with sensible default behavior or abstract methods, then let subclasses override responsibly. A closing question: when should the base class give a default implementation versus forcing the subclass to implement it? Method Overriding means subclasses replace or extend a base class method to provide specialized behavior while preserving a common api.. In practical terms, how subclasses provide specific behavior for inherited methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Method Overriding
Inheritance and specialization
class Animal:
  def speak(self):
    raise NotImplementedError("Subclasses must implement speak")

class Dog(Animal):
  def speak(self):
    return "Woof!"

class Cat(Animal):
  def speak(self):
    return "Meow!"
Here the base class declares the method and the subclasses override with concrete implementations, allowing polymorphic use via the shared API.
Notes & common pitfalls
  • Remember to call super() when you need to preserve base class behavior during override.
  • Use NotImplementedError in base methods to clearly indicate required overrides when not using ABCs.
  • Overriding without consistent signatures can break callers; keep parameters compatible.
Key Takeaway

Use overriding to specialize behavior while preserving a predictable interface for callers.

screens.title: Abstract Base Classes (ABCs)
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract Base Classes provide a way to declare explicit contracts in Python. While duck typing values behavior over explicit type, ABCs let you require certain methods at the class definition level. You create an abstract class by inheriting from ABC and marking methods with the @abstractmethod decorator. The concrete claim is: if a class does not implement all abstract methods, Python prevents instantiation and raises a TypeError. This enforces correctness earlier in development, which can be especially valuable in larger teams or plugin systems where missing implementations cause subtle runtime bugs. One subtle point is that ABCs do not eliminate polymorphism; they formalize it by ensuring required methods exist. Another nuance is that abstract classes may include concrete methods too — shared utility behavior can live in the abstract base and be reused. A common misconception is that ABCs are always necessary; often duck typing is sufficient for small-scale or exploratory code. The takeaway is to choose ABCs when you need enforceable contracts across multiple implementations, and use duck typing when you prefer lighter, faster iteration. In practical terms, why abcs exist and how they differ from duck typing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: ABCs let you enforce that subclasses implement specific methods, preventing instantiation when the contract is incomplete.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Abstract Base Classes
ABC Fundamentals
Use the abc module and @abstractmethod to declare methods that must be implemented by subclasses.
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def area(self):
    pass

  @abstractmethod
  def perimeter(self):
    pass
Attempting to instantiate Shape will raise a TypeError until concrete subclasses implement all abstract methods.
Why use ABCs?
  • Catch missing implementations at class instantiation time rather than later at runtime.
  • Provide a clear interface contract for teams and plugin architectures.
  • Allow shared concrete methods in the abstract class while enforcing key methods.
Key Takeaway

Choose ABCs to formalize behavior contracts when you need safety and clarity across implementations.

The lesson illustrates how the abc module prevents creating incomplete classes: if you forget to implement one of the methods, Python raises a TypeError when you attempt to instantiate the subclass. This enforces the design contract at the time of class instantiation, which is helpful in larger codebases. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Shape ABC Walkthrough
Full code from the chapter
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        """Calculates the area of the shape."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def perimeter(self):
        """Calculates the perimeter of the shape."""
        pass

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius):
        if radius <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Radius must be positive.")
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2

    def perimeter(self):
        return 2 * 3.14159 * self.radius

class Rectangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        if width <= 0 or height <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Width and height must be positive.")
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

    def area(self):
        return self.width * self.height

    def perimeter(self):
        return 2 * (self.width + self.height)
Example
Instantiate Circle and Rectangle after they implement required methods and call area and perimeter on each.
Common error
Trying to instantiate Shape directly raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape with abstract methods area, perimeter.
Key Takeaway
ABCs enforce design contracts and surface missing implementations as TypeError during instantiation.

screens.title: TypeError and Common ABC Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When working with ABCs a familiar runtime signal is the TypeError raised when you attempt to instantiate a class that is still abstract. The error often reads: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape with abstract methods area, perimeter. This message tells you precisely which methods remain unimplemented. Common causes include forgetting to import ABC or @abstractmethod, omitting an implementation in a subclass, or adding a new abstract method to the base class without updating all subclasses. Another subtle pitfall is defining the abstract method but changing its signature in a subclass; Python treats it as a different method and the abstract contract may still be considered unfulfilled. Your debugging steps are: read the TypeError for the missing methods, inspect subclass definitions for matching names and signatures, and ensure the abc imports are correct. A helpful design choice is to run unit tests that instantiate each concrete subclass and call required methods so you catch these errors in CI rather than during manual runs. Takeaway: ABCs make missing implementations visible early, but you must keep subclass signatures in sync. screens.title: Payment Processor Activity Overview
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to build a simple payment processor using an Abstract Base Class. Start by defining a PaymentMethod class that inherits from ABC and declares an abstract method process_payment(self, amount). Then implement two concrete subclasses: CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment. CreditCardPayment should accept card_number and expiry_date and its process_payment should print a message including the amount and card number. PayPalPayment should accept an email and its process_payment should print a message including the amount and the email. Finally, create instances of both classes, store them in a list, and iterate through the list calling process_payment on each entry. This demonstrates polymorphism: the loop treats each payment object uniformly and each concrete class responds with its own implementation. A common pitfall is forgetting the @abstractmethod decorator or not inheriting from ABC, which would remove the enforced contract. Another practical note: this activity is ideal for testing; write a small test that ensures each concrete class can be instantiated and that process_payment returns or prints the expected output. keyIdea.title: Activity outline
keyIdea.text: Create PaymentMethod ABC, implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment, then process a list of payment objects polymorphically.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Payment Processor Activity
Code Template
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class PaymentMethod(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        pass

class CreditCardPayment(PaymentMethod):
    def __init__(self, card_number, expiry_date):
        self.card_number = card_number
        self.expiry_date = expiry_date

    def process_payment(self, amount):
        print(f"Processing credit card payment of ${amount:.2f} for card {self.card_number} (expires {self.expiry_date}).")

class PayPalPayment(PaymentMethod):
    def __init__(self, email):
        self.email = email

    def process_payment(self, amount):
        print(f"Processing PayPal payment of ${amount:.2f} for account {self.email}.")

# Usage
credit_card = CreditCardPayment("1234-5678-9012-3456", "12/25")
paypal = PayPalPayment("user@example.com")

payment_methods = [credit_card, paypal]
for method in payment_methods:
    method.process_payment(100.50)
This template is the chapter’s activity: implement, instantiate, and iterate to demonstrate polymorphism with an enforced interface.
Checklist
  • Define PaymentMethod inheriting from ABC with @abstractmethod process_payment.
  • Implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment with required constructors.
  • Create instances, put them in a list, and call process_payment on each to demonstrate polymorphism.
Reflection
Think of a real-world scenario where enforcing a common interface would prevent errors better than relying solely on duck typing. Why?
Key Takeaway

Implementing ABCs in extensible systems gives you safety; polymorphism makes the system flexible to different implementations.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's pull the core concepts together. First, polymorphism allows different classes to respond to the same method call, enabling generic code that works across types. Second, duck typing in Python emphasizes behavior over declared types: if an object implements the required methods, code that expects those methods will work. Third, method overriding is how subclasses provide specific implementations for methods that appear in a base class, allowing specialization while preserving a shared A P I. These three ideas form the foundation of flexible object-oriented design in Python. Remember to document expected methods when relying on duck typing and to use ABCs when you need enforceable contracts. Use unit tests to validate concrete implementations and catch missing methods early. Finally, when designing systems like plugins or payment processors, balance the need for flexibility against the need for safety and choose the approach that best matches the team and runtime requirements.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two complementary ideas that make object-oriented Python code both flexible and reliable. First, polymorphism lets code operate on different kinds of objects through a shared behavior rather than a fixed type. Python’s dynamic duck typing is a practical example: if an object provides the methods your code needs, it will work regardless of the object's class. Second, Abstract Base Classes offer a stricter option when you need guarantees: they let you declare methods that every concrete subclass must implement, preventing accidental omissions. You will see simple, concrete examples: an animal speak demonstration that shows polymorphic calls in plain Python, operator behavior that adapts to operand types, and an ABC-based Shape example that demonstrates how the abc module and the @abstractmethod decorator protect your design. We will also practice by building a small payment processor that uses an abstract PaymentMethod interface. By the end of this chapter you’ll know when to rely on duck typing for fast, flexible code, and when to use ABCs to enforce contracts and catch errors early. Think about a plugin or payment system in your own projects and where each approach would fit.

Across these screens we'll set clear, measurable objectives. First, you will understand polymorphism: what it means for an object to take many forms and how method overriding and duck typing enable that in Python. Second, you will implement polymorphic behavior by designing common interfaces that different classes can share. Third, you will be able to explain why Abstract Base Classes exist and how the abc module provides the tools to define them. Finally on this screen you will practice defining and using abstract methods so concrete subclasses must implement specific behaviors. Each objective ties to a practical example: the animal speak example demonstrates duck typing, the Shape ABC shows enforcement, and the payment processor activity asks you to implement concrete payment classes. These objectives are chosen so you can both write flexible code when appropriate, and enforce contracts when correctness and safety matter. As you work through examples, reflect on when runtime flexibility is fine and when compile‑time guarantees avoid bugs. That reflection will guide your design decisions in real code.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical application and avoiding common errors. You will learn to apply polymorphism in real scenarios like plugin and strategy patterns where many implementations can be swapped without changing calling code. You will also practice writing concrete subclasses that satisfy abstract method requirements and observe the exact TypeError raised when you forget an implementation or instantiate an abstract class directly. Another objective is to recognize common pitfalls: forgetting to import ABC and abstractmethod, attempting to instantiate an abstract class, or overlooking required methods in subclasses. Finally, you'll build a small payment processor using an abstract PaymentMethod interface and two concrete classes to demonstrate polymorphic processing. These objectives emphasize both writing flexible code and guarding against mistakes that break runtime behavior. By reaching these milestones, you will be able to design components that are easy to extend and also resilient to developer omission.

Polymorphism literally means many forms. In programming that translates to the ability of different objects to respond to the same operation in their own way. In Python this is most often expressed through duck typing. The essential claim of duck typing is that you do not need the object to be of a particular declared type; you only need it to provide the required behavior. A concise concrete example is animals with a speak method. A Dog, Cat, and Duck all implement speak in their own way. A generic function that calls speak on a passed object will produce different results depending on the object's implementation, and that is polymorphism in action. One common misconception is thinking polymorphism requires inheritance. It does not: two unrelated classes that both implement the same method are polymorphic for the purposes of code that calls that method. Another contrast is static typed languages where interfaces or base classes are often declared ahead of time; Python prefers behavior over formal type declarations but still allows structured enforcement when needed. A practical takeaway is to design small, well-documented method contracts so callers can rely on behavior. Question for reflection: when would you prefer the freedom of duck typing over the assurance of an enforced interface?

Let's walk through the make_animal_speak example line by line and see how Python resolves the call at runtime. The function takes a parameter called animal and calls the speak method. Python looks up the attribute speak on the passed object and then executes the bound method. The important observation is that lookup happens on the concrete object, not on the expected type. In practice this means the same function adapts to any object that exposes the method. A concrete scenario: you may have a list of different device objects that all implement a status method; a single monitoring loop can call status on each device without type checks. A common error is assuming that duck typing eliminates the need for documentation. In reality you should document the expected methods and their signatures so callers and implementers agree. Another pitfall is assuming a missing method will raise a friendly error; instead Python will raise an AttributeError at the point of use. A practical debugging approach is to rely on tests that instantiate representative concrete types and call the shared A P I. Takeaway: duck typing is powerful, but document and test the method contract to avoid runtime surprises.

Python supports polymorphic operator behaviour through special methods. That means an operator such as plus or multiply delegates to a method like add or mul on the left operand. For built-in types this implements sensible behaviours: plus adds numbers and concatenates strings. You can also implement these special methods in your own classes to make operators behave meaningfully for custom types. A concrete example: implementing add for a Vector class so that the plus operator returns a new vector. A common misconception is that operator overloading magically makes code clearer. Overloading should be used to express natural arithmetic or combination semantics; otherwise it can confuse readers. When you design special methods, document their expected semantics and ensure they follow usual conventions like returning a new object for immutable types. In addition to add, methods like str and repr also shape how objects present themselves. The takeaway is to use operator overloading to make domain objects feel native to Python, but prefer explicit method names when behaviour could be surprising. Operator Overloading and Special Methods means operators call special methods on operands; classes can implement these to customize operator behaviour.. In practical terms, how operators adapt to operand types and how classes can customize behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Method overriding is a focused form of polymorphism: a subclass provides its own implementation of a method that is defined in a superclass. This allows a generic base class to declare an operation and concrete subclasses to tailor the implementation. For example, a base Animal class might define a speak method that raises NotImplementedError or provides a generic behavior; Dog and Cat subclasses override speak with concrete sounds. Unlike duck typing, overriding typically involves an inheritance relationship, but the idea remains the same: different objects respond in different ways to the same method call. One misconception is to override methods without calling the superclass when the superclass contains important initialization or shared behavior; in such cases you should call super(). Another nuance is that overriding can be used to specialize validation or error checking while still reusing shared logic. The practical pattern is to design base classes with sensible default behavior or abstract methods, then let subclasses override responsibly. A closing question: when should the base class give a default implementation versus forcing the subclass to implement it? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Abstract Base Classes provide a way to declare explicit contracts in Python. While duck typing values behavior over explicit type, ABCs let you require certain methods at the class definition level. You create an abstract class by inheriting from ABC and marking methods with the @abstractmethod decorator. The concrete claim is: if a class does not implement all abstract methods, Python prevents instantiation and raises a TypeError. This enforces correctness earlier in development, which can be especially valuable in larger teams or plugin systems where missing implementations cause subtle runtime bugs. One subtle point is that ABCs do not eliminate polymorphism; they formalize it by ensuring required methods exist. Another nuance is that abstract classes may include concrete methods too — shared utility behavior can live in the abstract base and be reused. A common misconception is that ABCs are always necessary; often duck typing is sufficient for small-scale or exploratory code. The takeaway is to choose ABCs when you need enforceable contracts across multiple implementations, and use duck typing when you prefer lighter, faster iteration.
